common_name: Koyo Azalea (Large Pink-and-Red Satsuki Sport of Suisen, Parent of Karenbana)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5-6.0), humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Koyo was registered in Japan in 1992 as a sport of the influential cultivar Suisen and has since been used in more than a dozen Satsuki breeding crosses, including the cross that produced Karenbana.

directions: Koyo arose as a spontaneous color sport of Suisen, one of the most heavily used parent cultivars in modern Satsuki breeding, and carries large flowers with a pink ground overlaid by red secondary markings rather than Suisen's red-on-white variegated pattern. Nursery records describe it as a confirmed mixoploid, a chromosomal quirk sometimes associated with sported azaleas that keep producing fresh color variation in their own offspring. Growers have used Koyo as a parent in well over a dozen registered crosses, among them Karenbana, making it an important link in the Juko-Suisen Satsuki breeding lines even though it is less commonly offered outside specialist collections. Like other Satsuki selections it flowers later in the season than Kurume or Southern Indica azaleas, so prune only right after bloom finishes since next year's flower buds set soon afterward.

common_name: Hakurin Azalea (Small White-and-Purple Satsuki Sport of Korin, Parent of Aiko)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5-6.0), humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Hakurin is a Japanese-bred sport of the cultivar Korin and was later crossed with Karenko to raise the hybrid Aiko.

directions: Hakurin produces small, star-shaped flowers with a white ground lightly marked in purple, a cooler and more sparing color pattern than many showier Satsuki selections. Its name, built from the characters for white, points to that pale dominant flower tone even though purple flecking and occasional darker sectors can appear within a single truss. It arose in Japan as a sport of the cultivar Korin, sharing that origin with the related sport Hikorin, and growers later used it as the white-flowered parent crossed with Karenko pollen to produce the hybrid Aiko. As with other Satsuki azaleas it blooms later in the season than Kurume or Southern Indica types and its compact, small-leaved habit makes it a popular subject for bonsai training as well as border and container planting.

common_name: Mibu-no-Hana Azalea (Large Pink-and-Red Satsuki Sport of Eiga-no-Homare, Parent of Masazuki)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5-6.0), humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Mibu-no-Hana was registered in Japan in 1989 as a sport of Eiga-no-Homare and was later used as the pollen parent of the hybrid Masazuki.

directions: Mibu-no-Hana carries large flowers with a pink ground overlaid by red secondary markings, a pattern it inherited through a long line of sported mutations traced back through Eiga-no-Homare to older foundational Satsuki cultivars. It was registered in Japan in 1989 and has since served as a breeding parent in its own right, most notably as the pollen parent behind the 2003 hybrid Masazuki, as well as in crosses that produced Kamon, Bikokan, and Shisui-no-Kagayaki. Detailed accounts of its bloom timing and mature plant size are scarce outside specialist Satsuki references, but as with its relatives in the Eiga-no-Homare line it can be expected to flower later in the season than Kurume or Southern Indica azaleas. Grow it as any other Satsuki selection, pruning only immediately after flowering since next year's buds set soon afterward.

common_name: Southern Star Pink Mexican Petunia (Compact Seed-Grown Ruellia)

planting.note: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant out once nights stay reliably above 50F; breeder trial data lists an 8-to-10-week finish time from transplant to flowering gallon-size plants, and in zone 9 and warmer 'Southern Star Pink' persists and spreads as a perennial.

directions: Southern Star Pink is the pastel-pink color in PanAmerican Seed's Southern Star line, marketed as the first dwarf Mexican petunia bred to finish reliably from seed rather than from cuttings. Funnel-shaped flowers open pale pink with a deeper carmine throat over a tidy, well-branched mound that stays under a foot tall, holding its compact form through summer heat better than older, taller Ruellia selections. It blooms from late spring through late summer and tolerates both soggy and dry spells once established, making it a dependable choice for mixed containers or mass bedding in hot climates. Because Ruellia simplex in all its forms is classified as a Category I invasive species by the Florida Exotic Pest Plant Council, gardeners in Florida and similarly humid regions should watch nearby areas for self-sown seedlings.
